Chapter 1 · The last morning

Today, no help. You already have everything you need.

Ten sessions ago, a house was born in the biggest building year America ever had, and a room full of strangers gave her a name. Since then she has been emptied, served, ordered, worked on, read, and billed. Today there is no new teaching first. The class proves — from memory, with no notes open — that the learning stayed.

Memory is the proof. If the chain comes back in order, everything after it is earned.

Her name first — confirmed, never re-chosen

Before anything is tested, say her name out loud. If your class named her in Class 1, tap it or type it here so it rides on this page too — the same name, carried into the last class exactly as it was carried into every class between.

That's her — the 1972 house. Same house, last chapter.
Say it in class

“Today, no help. You have everything you need already.”

How this last class runs — and why it starts empty-handed
The design of the day — from the programme blueprint, Session 10

If this is all new to you

Think of the difference between recognising a song and singing it. For nine classes, the trainees have recognised everything with the page open in front of them. Today the page shuts. Whatever they can still sing is theirs; whatever they can't was only ever borrowed. That is not cruelty — it is the honest way to find out what the course actually left behind.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The class rebuilds the whole journey from memory, Session 1 to Session 9, in order.
  2. The teacher closes the money story Session 9 opened — how money ends, not just how it leaks.
  3. A brand-new case, on a house the class has never met, is judged with no help at all.
  4. The class builds the lifecycle checklist itself, owns each role in one line, and graduates.

If you've done this work before

You already know why the order matters: a worker who can only perform with the checklist open is fine on a calm day and dangerous on a strange one. The strange day is the whole point of this session — a house across town, evidence that doesn't line up, and nobody senior in the room. Judgment that survives that is the product of the other nine classes.

The line to remember: “If you can say it with the book shut, it's yours. If you can't, you only borrowed it.”

The proof — what this session is built on

This page follows the programme's own Session 10 blueprint line for line: the retrieval opener, the closing of the money story, the unseen case with its expert verdict, the Update Line, and the graduation. The case, the worked money examples, and every figure in them are teaching examples, made up and labelled as such in the notes — the rules they demonstrate are the programme's standing rules.

If this is all new to you

“Correct only the order” sounds strange until you try it. If a trainee tells the journey in their own clumsy words but every link sits in the right place, the learning is real — they understand the chain. If the words are beautiful and two links are swapped, something was memorised, not understood. Today, sequence is the test; phrasing is free.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Notes shut, pages down. The teacher names the task: the whole journey, told back.
  2. The class builds it aloud, correcting each other as they go.
  3. When it stalls, the teacher offers exactly one word — “auction,” “permission,” “proof” — and steps back.
  4. The teacher corrects a link only when it lands in the wrong place in the chain.

If you've done this work before

The hardest discipline in this session is the teacher's silence. Every instinct says to rescue a stalling class with the answer. Resist it: the stall is the diagnostic. Where the chain breaks in the telling is exactly where the next real file would break in the office — better found here, out loud, than alone at a desk in month one.

The line to remember: “Don't correct the wording. Correct the order. If the chain is in order, the learning is real.”

The proof — where the rule comes from

The one-word prompt and the order-only correction are written into the Session 10 blueprint's retrieval section, alongside the full journey the class is expected to rebuild. The next slide lays that journey out in full, so you can check their telling against it link by link.

Chapter 2 · Retrieval

Nine classes. One house. Tell it back.

No notes, no pages, no peeking. The class rebuilds the whole wall map from memory — how she was born, how the loop broke, the long road she travelled, the system that stepped in, the work, the reading of her, and the money. One chain, in order, in their own words.

If a link is missing, the teacher gives one word — and nothing more.

1 · Born1972, the biggest total building year — loans, laws, cars, highways, zoning, and a filter

2 · The loop breaksPrice fall + payment shock — the family stops paying

3 · The roadLoss mitigation first, then foreclosure, auction, REO or agency home

Say it in class

“Tell it back to me — the whole journey, in order, in your own words. I will only stop you if a link lands in the wrong place.”

The journey in full — for checking their telling, link by link

If this is all new to you

Read these four links as one short film. A house is built in a year when a whole country is building — because loans got safe, babies grew up, and roads and rules made suburbs possible, while maps and deed rules quietly kept many families out. Then the money under the house breaks before the house does: prices fall, a payment jumps or a wage vanishes, and the family stops paying. The law insists help is tried first. Only then comes foreclosure, an auction nobody wins, and a bank — or the agency that insured the loan — owning a house it never wanted. And an empty house does not wait politely: it decays, week by week, all by itself.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Born (Session 1): boom babies forming households; FHA insurance and the GI Bill; Levitt's factory streets; highways, cars, utilities, air conditioning, tax help — and redlining and covenants filtering who could buy.
  2. The loop breaks (Session 2): jobs → rates → rules → building → back to jobs; the break is a price fall plus a payment shock, and the name for what follows is default.
  3. The road (Session 3): loss mitigation first — forbearance, modification, short sale, deed-in-lieu — under the federal floor that foreclosure generally cannot start before the loan is more than 120 days behind; then foreclosure by state law, auction, the lender's credit bid, REO or agency home.
  4. Vacancy (Session 3): week 1 the lawn and mail signal empty; weeks 2–4 water gets in; month 2 mold; month 3 onward stripping and blight. Vacancy itself is damage.

If you've done this work before

Listen, while they tell it, for the two confusions nine classes were built to kill: a filing treated as a house taken, and the combined foreclosure-plus-REO pile quoted as one number. If either survives into this telling, it will survive into their first month of files. Correct those two on the spot — gently, and as order errors, because that is what they are.

The line to remember: “Built by forces, emptied by a broken loop, carried down one road, in one order.”

The proof — the numbers inside these links

The figures the telling leans on were each proven in their own class: the 1972 total peak of 2,379,000 starts (1,309,000 single-family + 1,070,000 multifamily), the 2005 single-family peak of 1,716,000, the 2009 trough of 554,000, the roughly 76 million boom babies of 1946–1964, and the two agency piles of 2010 kept apart — Fannie Mae 166,787 and Freddie Mac 74,897. Sources for each live in the drawers of Classes 1 to 4; today they are recalled, not re-proven.

If this is all new to you

These five links are the working half of the story. A servicer cannot staff crews in fifty states, so the work travels down a chain of companies — that is structural, not laziness. An order then lives a whole life of its own, from the day it arrives to the day its payment is followed up. The work itself is five jobs, each with a clear picture of “done.” Reading a house is a skill with an order: name it, prove it, measure it — after safety, before everything. And money is a staircase a dollar walks down, losing a little at every step, with a named person responsible for each leak.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The system (Session 4): outsourcing because fifty states cannot be staffed from one office; nationals grow with the 2008 flood — Safeguard the labelled example, bought and renamed in 1990, never the founder; proof grows stricter; rules arrive — permission first, proof always.
  2. The first order (Session 5): the lifecycle — order, intake, permission gate, dispatch, field, proof, quality control, invoice, submission, payment, follow-up — and a class that held its own first order rather than approve a house that might still be lived in.
  3. The work (Sessions 6–7): grass is the house's face; secure is the permission slip for every job after it; winterization that never fakes a failed test; debris measured honestly in cubic yards; inspection where the report is the product.
  4. Reading her (Session 8): five kinds of damage, five house systems, and the skill in its fixed order — identify, document, quantify — with safety before tidy, always.
  5. The money (Session 9): BID → ALLOWABLE → APPROVED → INVOICED → PAID; a bid is scope + rate + evidence; and three people — Vendor Manager, Processor, Client Manager — carry one file from order to cash.

If you've done this work before

Notice what this half of the chain is really made of: not tools, but handoffs. Every link is a moment where one person's finished work becomes another person's starting evidence. That is why the capstone case later today is not about mowing or locks at all — it is about whether the handoffs hold when the evidence doesn't. If the class tells links 5–9 as a list of jobs instead of a chain of custody, prompt once: “Who hands what to whom?”

The line to remember: “The first half is how she fell. The second half is who catches her — and how.”

The proof — the chain on the wall

Underneath the whole journey sits the chain that has hung on the wall since Class 1, and the telling should land on it: Bank → Servicer → National → Our office → Field crew. One work order travels all five links before a single lock is changed. If the class can rebuild both chains — the house's journey and the order's journey — the wall has done its work.

Chapter 3 · Money's end

The file comes back. Now what?

Session 9 followed the money down the staircase and named every leak. But a class that only knows how money leaks does not yet know how money ends. It ends here — in the weeks after submission, when files come back, payments crawl, and every dollar that didn't arrive has to be explained. First: the rejection.

A rejection is not an argument to win. It is a gap to close — with evidence.

Say it in class

“Fix it with evidence and send it again. Never argue without proof.”

The rejection, taken apart

If this is all new to you

A rejection means the client sent the file back saying something is wrong — a photo missing, a date-stamp absent, a quantity they won't accept. It feels personal. It isn't. The file is a bundle of proof, and the client is saying one piece of proof failed. The fix is never a better argument; it is the missing piece of evidence, supplied properly, and the file sent again.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The file is submitted in the client portal and the client reviews it.
  2. It comes back rejected, with a reason — sometimes plain, sometimes buried (Slide 6 shows where reasons hide).
  3. The gap is fixed with evidence: the real photo taken, the real correction made — never written around.
  4. The file is resubmitted, and the cycle repeats until it is accepted or honestly closed.

If you've done this work before

The leak from Session 9's staircase lives here in the wild: of the last-step $150 that never arrived in that worked example, $60 was a rejection nobody fixed. Not rejected-and-impossible — rejected and abandoned. An unfixed rejection is the only leak that is pure choice, which is why it is taught first in money's end: before the wait, before the matching, close the loop you can actually close.

The line to remember: “A rejection is a gap with a name. Close the gap, keep the proof, send it again.”

The proof — where this sits in the money story

The worked staircase from Session 9, recalled exactly: bid 1,000 → allowable 800 → approved 700 → invoiced 700 → paid 550, all of it a labelled teaching example. The final $150 gap was itemised as $60 rejection never fixed, $50 short-paid, $40 property adjustment. Slides 3, 6, and 7 of this class take those three items one at a time and close them.

If this is all new to you

Picture two replies to the same rejection. Reply one: three paragraphs explaining how hard the crew worked and how unfair the decision feels. Reply two: one line — “Back-door lock, after photo attached” — and the photo. Only one of those files gets paid. The client never saw the effort; the client only ever sees the proof. Judge the evidence, not the effort — that sentence runs this whole session.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The rejection arrives and names — or hides — what's missing.
  2. The temptation is to defend the work that was done.
  3. The discipline is to supply the proof that was missing.
  4. Only when the proof genuinely cannot exist does the loss get a reason code instead (Slide 6).

If you've done this work before

There is a second trap hiding inside the first: resubmitting the same file louder — same photos, new cover note. Reviewers read that as noise, and the file's credibility pays for it. A resubmission should be visibly different in exactly the place the rejection pointed at, and identical everywhere else. Surgical, not emotional.

The line to remember: “Judge the evidence, not the effort. Good effort with bad proof still waits.”

One honest note

Not every rejection can be fixed. Sometimes the photo was never taken and the moment has passed; sometimes the work itself fell outside the rulebook. The honest end for those is not a louder argument — it is a reason code, owned and recorded, which is exactly where Slide 6 goes.

Chapter 4 · Money's end

Sixty days is not late. Sixty days is the road.

The file is accepted. Then — silence. Week after week of it. New workers panic here, and panic makes mistakes: chasing clients, mislabelling good money as lost, crying delinquency at a payment that is simply still travelling. On these orders, payment takes about sixty days to arrive. Younger than that is lag — the normal travel time of money. It is not delinquency, and it is not a loss.

The job during the wait has a name, and it is not “worry.”

Say it in class

“Tracking, not panic. A payment younger than sixty days is lag — the normal travel time of money — not delinquency.”

Lag, delinquency, and the discipline between them

If this is all new to you

Post a letter and it takes days to arrive — nobody calls the letter “lost” on day two. Money on these orders travels the same way, only slower: submission, review, approval, release, transfer. About sixty days end to end is the standing expectation in this operation. Until that window passes, an unpaid invoice is a letter in the post. After it passes with no payment and no explanation — now you have a real question to chase.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The file is submitted and accepted; the clock starts.
  2. Days 1–60: the payment is in the pipeline. The work is tracking — the file stays on the list, watched, dated, unhurried.
  3. Day 60 and beyond: an unpaid, unexplained balance graduates from lag to a genuine follow-up.
  4. Whatever the outcome, it ends in a match or a reason — never in a shrug (Slides 5 and 6).

If you've done this work before

The sixty-day rule protects two things at once. It protects the client relationship — an office that chases day-20 payments teaches the client to ignore its day-70 ones. And it protects the ledger: money written off in panic at day 30 has a way of arriving at day 55 into a file already closed wrong. Patience here is not temperament; it is bookkeeping hygiene.

The line to remember: “Young money is travelling money. Old, silent money is a question.”

One honest note

The sixty-day figure is this operation's standing rule for these clients, taught as the programme's rule — not a law of the industry. Other clients and other rulebooks run other clocks. As always in this course: the governing rulebook is the one on the order, and the wait is read against it.

If this is all new to you

Tracking is not staring at a balance. It is keeping every submitted file on a list with three things beside it: when it was submitted, when its sixty days run out, and what state it is in — waiting, matched, or needing a reason. Ten quiet minutes with that list each week is worth more than a panicked day at day 90, because the list catches the one file in fifty that truly has gone wrong while the other forty-nine were just travelling.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Every submission is logged with its date and property address.
  2. The list is reviewed on a rhythm — weekly is the programme's habit for the unexplained queue.
  3. Payments that land are matched off the list (next slide shows how).
  4. Anything past its window without payment or explanation moves to follow-up, then to a reason code.

If you've done this work before

Hold the distinction that saves the most grief in a real office: “not yet paid” is a status, “unpaid” is a conclusion. Statuses are updated; conclusions are defended. The trainee who learns to say “day 41, still inside the window, no action needed” in a status meeting has understood this slide better than the one who presents the same file as a problem.

The line to remember: “A list watched weekly beats a panic monthly — every time.”

The proof — where the sixty days sits

The wait belongs to the Client Manager's workflow from Session 9: submit in the client portal → track the review → fix rejections with evidence → follow the chains → wait about sixty days → match payments → account for losses. This slide teaches the fifth step; the next two slides teach the sixth and seventh.

Chapter 5 · Money's end

The payment arrived — under a different number.

Here is the trap that manufactures fake losses. An order is submitted and shows no payment — ever. The office marks it unpaid. But the client answered that order with a follow-up order at the same property, under a different number, and paid under the new one. The old order was not unpaid. It was superseded — replaced. Work-order numbers differ from system to system. The address does not.

Match payments to properties, not to numbers — or the ledger fills with losses that never happened.

Say it in class

“Never call an order unpaid until you have checked the chain. Match by address, not by number.”

The chain, worked slowly
Teaching example — made up, labelled, the pattern is the lesson

If this is all new to you

Imagine the office submits work under Order A for a house. Weeks pass; Order A shows no payment at all. It is tempting to write “unpaid” and move on. But look at the property, not the order: the client opened Order B at the very same address — a follow-up — and the money arrived under B. One job, two numbers, one payment. The order numbers are labels each system sticks on the work; the address is the house itself, and the house is what got paid for.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Order A is submitted for the property. No payment ever shows against A.
  2. Before anything is called unpaid, the chain check runs: search the same address for follow-up orders.
  3. Order B is found at that address — a different number, possibly a different number again in the client portal than in the office engine.
  4. Payment is sitting under B. Order A is recorded as superseded — in the reason codes of the next slide, that is CHAIN-PAID.

If you've done this work before

You have lived the uglier version of this: a renumbered order looks, to a number search, like one job that vanished and a stranger job that appeared from nowhere. Whole afternoons die reconciling ghosts like that. The address-first habit is not pedantry — it is the difference between a ledger that describes houses and a ledger that describes paperwork. Houses are what the money was for.

The line to remember: “Numbers are labels. The address is the house. Pay follows the house.”

The proof — why numbers differ

The same job routinely carries one number in the office engine and another in the client portal, and a follow-up order at the same property carries a third. That is why the programme's matching rule is address-first, with work-order numbers treated as attributes that can differ per system — a rule the class first met in Session 9 and now applies as the money ends.

If this is all new to you

Think of it as a courtroom rule: “unpaid” is a verdict, and a verdict needs its evidence heard first. The chain check is that hearing. It takes minutes — pull the property by address, list every order ever opened there, and see whether the money landed under any of them. Only a property with no paying successor anywhere earns the harsher labels of the next slide.

How it happened, step by step

  1. A submitted order passes its window with no payment against its number.
  2. The chain check runs by address — every order at that property, in every system.
  3. If a successor was paid: the old order is CHAIN-PAID, superseded, closed honestly.
  4. If no successor exists: the loss moves on to a true reason — rejected, short-paid, unallowable — or into the unexplained queue to be hunted.

If you've done this work before

There is a discipline hiding in the sequencing: the chain check is cheap and the alternatives are expensive. Calling a client about a “missing” payment that arrived under another number spends trust the office will want back later, on a day the money really is missing. Check the address first — it is the thirty-second habit that keeps every later escalation believable.

The line to remember: “No ‘unpaid’ is final until the address has had its say.”

The proof — the rule, stated as the programme states it

From the Session 9 workflow, unchanged: a submitted order answered by a different order at the same property, paid under the new one, is never called “unpaid” until the chain is checked. Address is the key; numbers differ across systems. The old order's honest status is superseded — replaced, not unpaid.

Chapter 6 · Money's end

If you cannot name the reason, you have not finished the job.

Some money truly does not come back. That is a fact of the business — and it is not the end of the work. Every loss gets one reason, from one list, used the same way in every file. Five of the codes close a story. The sixth is not a story at all: it is a queue, and the queue is driven to zero.

REJECTEDSent back by the client and never fixed. The rejection stood; the money didn't move.
SHORT-PAIDPaid — but below the invoice, for a quantity or a line the client did not accept.
UNALLOWABLEThe work sat outside the rulebook on the order. No rulebook pays for it.
ADJUSTEDAbsorbed by a property-level adjustment at the same property — next slide.
CHAIN-PAIDPaid under a follow-up order at the same property. Superseded, not unpaid.
UNEXPLAINEDNo reason found yet. A queue — never a final answer. Driven to zero.
Say it in class

“Every loss gets a reason. UNEXPLAINED is a queue, never an answer.”

One list, everywhere — and where the reasons hide

If this is all new to you

Why codes at all? Because “we lost some money on that house” teaches nobody anything, while “SHORT-PAID — client rejected the debris quantity” teaches the next bid, the next crew, and the next invoice exactly what to change. A code turns a disappointment into an instruction. And the list only works if it is one list: the moment two desks use two lists, the totals stop meaning anything.

How it happened, step by step

  1. A payment lands short, or never lands, or a rejection is finally unfixable.
  2. The chain check runs first (last slide) — CHAIN-PAID is ruled in or out by address.
  3. The reason is hunted where reasons live: on the order's invoice section, beside the payment amounts.
  4. One code is recorded. If none fits yet, the loss enters UNEXPLAINED — visibly, on a list, with an owner.

If you've done this work before

A housekeeping note worth saying aloud: older drafts of this programme carried a code called UNKNOWN alongside these six. It is folded into UNEXPLAINED now — same queue, one name. If a trainee meets UNKNOWN in an old handout, they read it as UNEXPLAINED. Two names for one queue is how queues quietly double.

The line to remember: “One list, six codes, every file — or the numbers stop meaning anything.”

The proof — examples of each, from the teaching files

Rejected for a missing date-stamp and never fixed: REJECTED. Short-paid after an unapproved over-allowable: SHORT-PAID. Personal property hauled away though the order never listed it: UNALLOWABLE. A loss covered by money received but unspent at the same property: ADJUSTED. Paid under the follow-up order: CHAIN-PAID. And anything still being hunted: UNEXPLAINED — for now.

If this is all new to you

Picture a tray on the Client Manager's desk labelled “not yet explained.” A loss may sit in that tray — losses are allowed to be mysterious for a while. What it may not do is live there. Every week the tray is emptied by work: re-check the chain, re-read the invoice section, ask the question the file hasn't answered yet. A loss leaves the tray only by gaining a real code. Zero does not mean the losses vanished; it means none of them is nameless anymore.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Every unexplained loss is listed by property, its reason field honestly blank.
  2. The Client Manager owns the queue — one name, not “the office.”
  3. The queue is reviewed weekly; each entry gets a next action, not just a next look.
  4. Zero is reached when no blank reason fields remain — every loss coded, every dollar explained.

If you've done this work before

The reason this queue matters out of proportion to its dollars: it is where patterns hide. One unexplained loss is a mystery; nine unexplained losses sharing a crew, a rulebook, or a photo habit are a system fault wearing a disguise. The weekly review is not tidiness — it is the office's early-warning radar, and it only works while the queue is small enough to actually read.

The line to remember: “Unexplained is where a loss waits — not where it retires.”

One honest note

Reasons are genuinely hard to find — they sit on the work order's invoice section, beside the payment amounts, in a place most screens make easy to miss. That is why “no reason found” is only ever said after that section has actually been checked. A loss is not unexplained because nobody looked; it is unexplained after looking, and the looking is the job.

Chapter 7 · Money's end

Sometimes the money to cover a loss is already in the house.

Last piece of money's end. A property can hold money that was received but never spent — paid in, with no cost recorded against it — while the same property also carries a loss. Leaving the two sitting apart, unmatched, is how ledgers lie politely. The adjustment sets one against the other, at the same property — and nothing is booked until the owner approves it.

Received-but-unspent is not a bonus. It is a balance waiting for its other half.

Say it in class

“Money received but not spent on a property is set against that same property's losses — with the owner's approval before anything is booked.”

The adjustment, worked and guarded
Teaching example — made up, labelled, the pattern is the lesson

If this is all new to you

Keep it at kitchen-table level. On one property, the office was paid 500 for work, and the records show no cost was ever booked against that 500 — no crew paid from it, no expense tied to it. The same property also lost 300 somewhere else in its story. The adjustment says: let 300 of the in-hand 500 answer for the 300 loss. The loss gets the code ADJUSTED, and 200 remains received-but-unspent, still to be reconciled honestly another day. Nothing is invented; money is simply matched to its own house.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Receipts are matched to the property by address — the same key as the chain check.
  2. The received-but-unspent balance is confirmed: money in, no cost recorded.
  3. The same property's losses are listed beside it, each with its reason.
  4. The owner approves the adjustment. Only then is it booked, and the loss is coded ADJUSTED.

If you've done this work before

Two guards make this honest instead of convenient. First: same property, always — the moment unspent money from one address starts covering losses at another, the ledger stops describing houses and starts describing wishes. Second: owner approval before booking, every time — an adjustment moves money between stories, and that is precisely the class of decision this programme reserves upward. The trainee proposes; the owner disposes.

The line to remember: “Same property, owner's word, then booked — in that order, or not at all.”

The proof — the numbers, held apart

500Received at the property, no cost recorded against it
300Adjusted against that same property's loss
200Still received-but-unspent, still to reconcile

And recall where the idea first surfaced: in Session 9's staircase, $40 of the final $150 gap was exactly this — a property adjustment, money moved on the same property to cover another loss there. This slide is that line, taught in full.

If this is all new to you

An unmatched balance makes a property look richer than it is and its losses look lonelier than they are. Months later, nobody remembers which dollars belonged to which story, and the honest matching this slide teaches becomes archaeology. The rule exists so that never happens: a property's money and a property's losses are reconciled while both are still young enough to recognise each other.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Money arrives at a property with no cost recorded — it happens, through advances, corrections, and chain payments.
  2. It is flagged on receipt, not discovered by accident at year-end.
  3. It is held against that property only, awaiting the owner's decision.
  4. It leaves as an approved adjustment, a proper cost booking, or an explained balance — never as a mystery.

If you've done this work before

Notice how this closes the money story's moral arc. The staircase in Session 9 was about money leaking away step by step. Money's end is about the opposite failure: money arriving and being mishandled by inattention. Leaks and lumps — both are the same sin, an unexplained dollar. The graduate this course is building is simply a person who refuses to leave dollars unexplained, in either direction.

The line to remember: “Every dollar explained — leaking out or sitting still, no exceptions.”

The proof — where the adjustment sits in the codes

ADJUSTED is one of the six unified codes from the last slide, and it is the only one that closes a loss without new money arriving. That is exactly why it carries the heaviest guard: same property, address-matched, owner-approved. A loss coded ADJUSTED should always be traceable to the balance that covered it.

Chapter 8 · Money's end, last word

One last time: two systems, two hands, never mixed.

The teacher holds up two hands and names them apart, one final time. On one hand, the office engine — our own system, where the office builds the file: photos tagged, quantities entered, the invoice prepared. On the other, the client portal — the client's system, where the finished file is submitted and the client answers. Build in one. Submit in the other. Confusing them is how files get lost.

Kept apart one last time — because on day one of the real job, nobody will be standing there to separate them for you.

Say it in class

“The office engine is where we build the file. The client portal is where we submit it. Two systems — never confused.”

What lives in each hand

If this is all new to you

Think of a letter. The office engine is your desk at home: the letter is written there, the photos are paper-clipped in order, the address is checked, the envelope is sealed. The client portal is the post box on the corner: nothing is written there — finished letters are handed over there, and replies come back from there. Writing on the post box, or posting from your desk, are both nonsense. Each place has one job.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Office engine: photos and report come in; every photo is tagged to its line item and flagged Before / During / After; completion quantities are entered — never the bid or price columns; the invoice is built and checked.
  2. The gate between: the Processor prepares the file up to ready and stops. The owner marks Ready For Office himself — that stamp is never anyone else's to give.
  3. Client portal: the finished file is submitted there, on the owner's word, after his cross-check. Reviews, rejections, and payments are tracked from there.

If you've done this work before

You know the failure mode by heart: a correction typed into the wrong system, a file “submitted” that only ever existed on the office side, a rejection answered in a portal the client never reads. It is repeated in this last class not because it is complicated, but because it is the mistake that experience does not protect against — tired people mix systems, and the only cure is the habit being loud enough to survive a long day.

The line to remember: “Build it on our desk. Submit it in their box. Never the other way round.”

The proof — the sequence that guards both hands

The full submission sequence, which the class will say once more at graduation: complete the work → report the finished state → the owner cross-checks it himself → submit only on the owner's word. Every arrow in that sequence crosses from the office engine's world to the client portal's world exactly once — at the final step, and never before.

If this is all new to you

Stand back and look at what the last five slides actually built: a rejection answered with evidence, a wait read with a calendar instead of fear, a payment hunted by address, a loss named with a code, a balance matched at its own property, and two systems never confused. Six habits, one sentence. If a graduate carries nothing else into month one, this sentence alone will keep their ledger honest while the rest of the craft catches up.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Rejections: fix with evidence, resubmit — never argue without proof.
  2. The wait: sixty days is lag; tracking, not panic.
  3. Matching: by address, never by number alone; superseded is not unpaid.
  4. Losses: one code each, from one list; UNEXPLAINED is a queue driven to zero.
  5. Adjustments: same property, owner-approved, booked after — never before.

If you've done this work before

Money's end is deliberately taught after the staircase, not inside it. Knowing where money leaks is an analyst's skill; knowing what to do in the sixty quiet days afterwards is an operator's. This session graduates operators. If the class remembers the staircase but forgets the sentence, they will describe their losses beautifully — and change none of them.

The line to remember: “Every loss gets a reason, and unexplained is a queue driven to zero.”

The proof — money's end, complete

That is the whole of money's end, and the money story of the course is now closed: a bid built from scope + rate + evidence, walked down five rungs, and accounted for at the far end — every dollar paid, matched, coded, or queued by name. What remains today is not more teaching. It is proof. Next slide: the help stops.

Chapter 9 · The graduation proof

A new house. No help. Your call.

Now the help stops. This is a house across town — not the 1972 house, so no memory can carry anyone. The case is made up for teaching, labelled as such, and laid out exactly as a real file would arrive. The order: Secure + Winterize + Debris. Read the evidence. Decide — approve, hold, or reject — defend it in writing, and write an Update Line of twenty-five words or fewer. Alone first. Then in pairs. Then in writing.

The teacher says nothing during the writing except the time.

The file, exactly as it landed

Everything the class gets is on this board — nothing more is coming. Judge what is here, and notice what is not.

  • Secure: the crew changed the front-door lock. For the back-door lock there is no photo — only a wide shot of the back of the house, which proves nothing about the lock.
  • Winterize: the pressure test failed — the gauge would not hold. The crew wrote that a valve was stuck, and drained what they could. There is no photo of the meter after shutoff.
  • Debris: the pile measures 8 ft long × 5 ft wide × 3 ft high. The bill claims 9 cubic yards.
  • Debris, again: a television was hauled away. The order never listed a television.
  • By the back door: a dog bowl holds fresh water. And a car that sat in the driveway in the before photo has moved in the after photo.

Make the call — then check it against the verdict

Pairs decide first, out loud, and write their defence before touching a button below. The buttons are the reveal, not the decision: tap the verdict your pair chose and read honestly how it stands. The expert verdict — and the reasons that decide it — are on the next slide either way.

Say it in class

“Judge the evidence, not the effort. Good effort with bad proof still waits.”

Running the case — the rules of the next twenty minutes

If this is all new to you

Why alone first? Because the loudest voice in a pair becomes the pair's answer, and this exercise is hunting for each person's own judgment before it is socialised. Alone, a trainee discovers what they actually think. In pairs, they discover whether they can defend it. In writing, they discover whether it survives being read cold by someone who wasn't in the room — which is exactly how every real file is judged.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The case is handed out, labelled as made up, for a house the class has never met.
  2. Each trainee decides alone: approve, hold, or reject.
  3. Pairs compare, argue from the evidence board, and settle on one verdict.
  4. Each pair writes its defence, plus an Update Line of twenty-five words or fewer.
  5. Only when every pair has written does the teacher reveal the expert verdict — next slide.

If you've done this work before

Protect the silence during the writing. The urge to circulate, hint, and rescue is strongest precisely because the case is well built — it has one headline failure and three quieter ones, and watching a pair find the headline and miss the money is uncomfortable. Let them. The reveal lands ten times harder on a pair that wrote the wrong verdict in full sentences than on one that was steered to the right one.

The line to remember: “This proves judgment, not memory — and judgment is what's being graduated.”

The proof — what the writing must contain

The capstone pass standard, as the programme sets it (the teacher may adjust it): pass = the written defence names all four failures — permission uncertainty, proof gap, winterization test not honestly closed, money math — AND the Update Line passes its four checks. Revise-and-retry = three of four on either side. Not yet = fewer than three of four. The four failures and the four checks are the next two slides.

If this is all new to you

If this case were about the 1972 house, the class would “know” things that aren't in the evidence — her history, her street, how her story usually goes — and those memories would quietly fill the gaps in the file. That is the exact failure the case is designed to catch. In the real job, every house is a stranger's house. The file is all you get. Learning to judge from the file alone is the graduation.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Nine classes of story built familiarity — deliberately.
  2. The capstone removes that familiarity in one move: new house, new street, no back-story.
  3. What remains is transferable skill: permission, proof, honest tests, honest math.
  4. If those four survive the change of house, they will survive the change to a real caseload.

If you've done this work before

There is a quiet compliment to the class buried in this design, and it is worth saying at the reveal: the case is not a trick. Every signal on the board was taught, in plain sight, across Sessions 5 to 9 — occupancy signs, missing proof, the failed-test rule, the cubic-yard formula, the unallowable line. A pair that finds all four failures has not been lucky; they have been listening for ten sessions.

The line to remember: “If it only works on her, it isn't judgment yet. Today it has to work on a stranger.”

The proof — the case is synthetic, and says so

The unseen case is a made-up teaching case, labelled as such wherever it appears — no real property, order, or crew stands behind it. Its details are drawn from the programme's own blueprint for Session 10, including the order types, the evidence gaps, and the expert verdict on the next slide.

Chapter 10 · The reveal

The verdict is HOLD.

One headline reason, and three more failures behind it — and a written defence must name all four. The headline is permission: fresh water in a dog bowl and a car that moved are signs the house may still be lived in, and a house that may be lived in is never secured on a guess. HOLD — and escalate the occupancy question before any secure work is judged at all.

Say it in class

“A failed test is information, not failure. Report it — don't fake it.”

The four failures, and the steps that follow — in order

If this is all new to you

Two small details, one large meaning. A dog bowl with fresh water means an animal was cared for recently — someone has been here, lately, on purpose. A car that moved between the before and after photos means a person came and went during the work itself. Either sign alone deserves a pause. Together they say the one thing a secure crew must never ignore: this house may still be someone's home. Securing a lived-in house is the worst mistake in this business, and it is made by guessing past exactly these signs.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The evidence board is read for occupancy first — before locks, before tests, before money.
  2. Fresh water + moved car = occupancy uncertain. Not proven lived-in; not provably empty. Uncertain is enough.
  3. The verdict follows from the uncertainty, not from the other failures: HOLD.
  4. The occupancy question is escalated — handed upward to someone who can judge it — before any secure work is judged at all.

If you've done this work before

The question every class asks here, answered the way the blueprint answers it: “The front-door lock was already changed — isn't it too late to hold?” No. HOLD now means: hold all remaining work, hold the file — do not submit it, do not approve it — report the lock change that was already made, and escalate for instruction, including whether the lock should be restored. A hold after the fact cannot undo the lock change, but it stops every further harm and puts the decision with someone who can judge it. The permission check should have happened before the crew acted — that is the lesson, and it is better learned here than on a real doorstep.

The line to remember: “Uncertain occupancy is not a detail. It is the verdict.”

The proof — the defence sentence for this failure

In the model written defence, this failure carries the first clause: the file cannot be approved because permission is uncertain. It is named first because it outranks the other three — a file with perfect proof and perfect math still holds, if the house may be lived in.

If this is all new to you

Failure two is about what a photograph proves. A wide shot of the back of a house proves the house has a back. It does not prove a lock was changed — locks are small, and proof of a lock is a close photo of that lock. Failure three is subtler, and kinder to the crew: the pressure test failing is not the failure. The crew did the brave, correct thing by writing “valve stuck” instead of faking a pass. The failure is the unfinished honesty — no photo of the meter after shutoff — so the winterization was never honestly closed either way.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Back-door lock: changed or not, the file contains no photo that proves it. Proof gaps go back to the field — never papered over.
  2. Pressure test: the gauge would not hold; a valve was stuck; the crew drained what they could and wrote it down. Correct instincts, honestly recorded.
  3. But the meter after shutoff was never photographed, so the shutoff itself is unproven.
  4. Both gaps join the next-steps list: the missing lock photo and the meter photo come from the field, and the stuck valve is reported exactly as found.

If you've done this work before

Hold the two failures apart in the debrief, because they teach opposite lessons. The lock photo is a completeness failure — the proof habit from Sessions 5 and 6, broken. The winterization is a closure failure — the Session 7 rule (“a failed test is information, not failure”) half-kept: reported, yes; evidenced, no. Praising the crew's honesty while still holding the file is the exact tone a good reviewer strikes, and the class should hear it modelled.

The line to remember: “Reported honestly is half the job. Proven honestly is the whole job.”

The proof — the defence sentence for these failures

The model defence carries them in its middle clauses: proof is incomplete, and the winterization test was never honestly closed. Note what the defence does not say: it does not call the crew dishonest, and it does not call the winterization “failed” as a verdict on the crew. It names the state of the file — which is the only thing the writer of a defence actually knows.

If this is all new to you

Debris is measured the way Session 7 taught: length × width × height, in feet, divided by 27. This pile: 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cubic feet, and 120 ÷ 27 is about 4.4 — call it four and a half cubic yards. The bill claims 9: double the pile that exists. And the television is simpler still: the order never listed it, so hauling it is unallowable — outside what the order covered — and it comes off the bill entirely, however heavy it was.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Measure the pile from the file: 8 ft × 5 ft × 3 ft = 120 cubic feet.
  2. Convert: 120 ÷ 27 ≈ 4.4 cubic yards — about four and a half.
  3. Compare with the bill: 9 claimed against ~4.5 measured. The quantity is corrected to the measured figure.
  4. The television line is removed in full: unallowable — the order never covered it.

If you've done this work before

Resist the urge to call the 9 a lie. It may be a lie; it may be a second pile nobody photographed, a mis-measured height, or a copied line. The file cannot tell you, and the defence must not pretend it can. What the file proves is narrower and stronger: the billed quantity is not supported by the measured evidence. Correct it to the measured figure and let the field explain the rest — the same evidence-over-effort discipline as the rejections slide, now applied to arithmetic.

The line to remember: “Bill what you measured. Measure what you can prove.”

The proof — the defence, in full

The model written defence, all four failures in one breath: “The file cannot be approved because permission is uncertain, proof is incomplete, the winterization test was never honestly closed, and the money does not match the math.” And the next steps, fixed in order: escalate the occupancy check first; get the missing lock photo and the meter photo from the field; report the stuck valve exactly as found; correct the debris quantity to the measured figure; remove the television line. Only then does the file move again. Try the arithmetic yourself in the checker below.

Check the debris math yourself

The case pile, pre-filled. Change any side and watch the cubic yards move — then compare what the math says with the 9 the bill claimed. Length × width × height, in feet, divided by 27.

Chapter 11 · The graduation proof, part two

Twenty-five words. Four checks. No hiding.

Every verdict travels with a short written message — the Update Line — that the next person on the file reads first. It passes only four checks: the signal is named, the decision is stated, the next step is named, and it fits in twenty-five words or fewer. Short is not a style choice. Short is what gets read.

The model line is seventeen words long. The class counts them together.

Say it in class

“If you cannot name the reason, you have not finished the job.”

Draft your pair's Update Line here

Type the line your pair wrote for the unseen case. The counter keeps the twenty-five-word limit honest — the other three checks are yours to judge with the cards beneath.

1 · Signal namedWhat was seen — the fresh bowl, the moved car, the missing photo, the failed test.
2 · Decision statedThe verdict itself, in the line — HOLD, in this case, in capital letters and first.
3 · Next step namedWhat happens now — escalate occupancy; fix proof and math.
4 · Twenty-five or fewerThe model line is 17 words. Count them with the class, out loud, together.
The model line, taken apart word by word

If this is all new to you

Read the line the way its reader will: standing in an office, forty files deep, deciding what happens next in the next ten seconds. “HOLD” lands first — the decision before the reasons, because the decision is what's acted on. Then four signals in nine words, each one a fact from the evidence board, none of them an opinion. Then the orders: escalate, fix, fix. A stranger could run this file from this line alone. That is the standard.

How it happened, step by step

  1. Count it with the class: HOLD(1) dog(2) bowl(3) fresh(4) car(5) moved(6) lock(7) photo(8) missing(9) pressure(10) failed(11) Escalate(12) occupancy(13) fix(14) proof(15) and(16) math(17). Seventeen.
  2. Check one — signal: four signals named, in the order the verdict ranked them.
  3. Check two — decision: HOLD, stated, first word.
  4. Checks three and four — next steps named (escalate, fix proof, fix math), inside the limit with eight words to spare.

If you've done this work before

Notice what the model line leaves out, because trainees always ask: no crew names, no blame, no “unfortunately,” no history of the case. An Update Line is not a report and not a defence — the defence lives in the written verdict; the line is a signpost. Every word spent on colour is a word stolen from signal, and the twenty-five-word wall is what enforces the trade.

The line to remember: “Decision first, signals second, steps third — and stop.”

The proof — the pass standard, joined up

The Update Line is half the capstone standard: pass requires all four failures named in the written defence AND this line passing all four checks. A pair can therefore hold the right verdict and still be sent back to revise — on a line that buries its decision, or runs to forty words. That is deliberate: in the real job, the line is what the next desk acts on, and a verdict nobody can find in the writing changes nothing.

If this is all new to you

This is the programme's scripted check for this session — the fast version of the whole capstone, usable in any spare minute. Two signals are given; the trainee must produce the verdict and defend it in one sentence. A good answer sounds like: “Hold — because fresh water and a moved car mean the house may still be lived in, and permission comes before everything.” Verdict, signal, rule. Three beats.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The teacher reads the two signals aloud, nothing else.
  2. Thirty seconds in pairs — the standard rhythm of every check in this course.
  3. One answer aloud, defended in a single sentence.
  4. The teacher corrects the reasoning only if the verdict or the because is missing.

If you've done this work before

Keep this check in your pocket after graduation day, because it is built to travel: a trainer can run it in a corridor, a team lead can run it over a photo set, and it still tests the exact judgment the job runs on. If a room full of graduates answers it instantly and correctly a month from now, the capstone did its work.

The line to remember: “Two signals, one verdict, one because.”

The proof — where the check comes from

The scripted check is written into the Session 10 blueprint word for word — “Dog bowl fresh, car moved — HOLD, approve, or reject? Defend it in one sentence.” — as this session's example of the course-wide rhythm: a two-minute check at least every ten minutes, so no stretch of teaching ever runs long without the class doing something with it.

Chapter 12 · The end — and the beginning

She is a home again. And the story restarts.

The last part of the session belongs to the class, not the teacher. Together they build the lifecycle as a checklist and take ownership of it, line by line — then each role is owned in one line, the guarding sequence is said one final time, and the 1972 house is sold to a new family. New curtains go up. A new name goes on the mailbox. And somewhere else, another house is already waiting for the next class.

Say it in class

“Complete the work, report the finished state, the owner cross-checks, and submit only on the owner's word.”

1Order — it arrives, and it is read, not skimmed.
2Intake — the file is opened whole, in the office engine.
3Permission gate — occupancy judged before anything else moves.
4Dispatch — the right crew, the right house, the exact scope.
5Field — the work done as ordered, safety before tidy.
6Proof — before, during, after; every claim photographed.
7Quality control — gaps go back to the field, never papered over.
8Invoice — honest quantities, the rulebook on the order as boss.
9Submission — in the client portal, on the owner's word only.
10Payment — waited for, tracked, matched by address.
11Follow-up — chains checked, every loss given its reason.
The roles, owned in one line each — and what the class proved

If this is all new to you

Learn the three lines as one sentence with three owners. The Vendor Manager gets the right crew to the right house with permission. The Processor turns proof into a clean, honest invoice. The Client Manager turns the invoice into cash — and explains every dollar that did not come back. Every failure in the unseen case belonged to one of those lines, and every next step does too.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The class builds the lifecycle checklist above together, line by line, in their own words where they can.
  2. Each role is then claimed aloud, one line per role — the handoff line from Session 9, now spoken as a promise.
  3. The teacher closes the guarding sequence one final time: complete → report → owner cross-checks → submit on the owner's word.
  4. And the boundary inside it is named plainly: the owner marks Ready For Office himself. That stamp is never anyone else's to give.

If you've done this work before

The sentence the teacher saves for this exact moment, from the blueprint: “No single role sees what you now see.” Each desk in a real office sees its slice — the crew, the proof, the money. This class has walked the whole file end to end, which is precisely what makes a graduate useful across desks instead of only on one. Say it slowly; it is the closest thing this course has to a diploma line.

The line to remember: “No single role sees what you now see.”

The proof — the graduation proof itself

The memory anchor of this session is not a fact or a figure. It is the case the class judged cold — a stranger's house, no help, a verdict defended in writing and compressed into seventeen honest words. Anchors from earlier classes were things: a name, a drawn loop, a road of cards. This one is a demonstration, and it is the only kind that survives contact with a real caseload.

If this is all new to you

Every earlier class ended on a hook — a question pulling the story forward. This one refuses to, on purpose. The house's story is complete: born, lived in, emptied, served, judged, and lived in again. What continues is not her story but the pattern — the same cycle, already turning on another street, around a house whose name some future class will choose in its first ten minutes.

How it happened, step by step

  1. The lifecycle is owned, the roles are claimed, the sequence is said one last time.
  2. The class returns to the house they named in Class 1 — and lets her go.
  3. She is sold; a new family hangs curtains and puts a new name on the mailbox.
  4. The teacher's last word is not a summary but a handover: the next empty house is already out there.

If you've done this work before

End on time, and end plainly. The temptation at a capstone is a speech; the blueprint asks for something better — the checklist, the roles, the sequence, and the door closing on the story. Graduates remember rituals longer than remarks. Let the last thing they do be the work itself, done one final time, together, in order.

The line to remember: “Built, lived in, aged, broken, emptied, owned by paper, kept alive by people, lived in again.”

The proof — ten classes, one chain

The chain from Class 1's first slide, completed: boom → suburb → ageing → default → vacancy → REO → preservation → home again. In Class 1 it was a promise about where the story would go. Today every link of it has been taught, practised, and — in the unseen case — judged without help. The retrieval at this session's open is also its close: the whole journey, told back one final time, needs no notes anymore.

Arrow keys work too. The full notes on each slide carry the basics, the steps, the evidence, and the line to say.

All slides — Class 10

The full arc of the capstone on one screen — memory first, money's end, the unseen case judged cold, and graduation. Tap any slide to jump to it.

The logic behind this class

Why Class 10 is built the way it is, what its cases do — and don't — prove, and how to run it. One teacher to another, before the class walks in.

Why the last class teaches almost nothing new

Nine classes built a chain: a house's journey from birth to vacancy, and an order's journey from arrival to payment. A tenth class of new material would test whether trainees can keep up. This one tests something more valuable — whether they can judge. So Class 10 is built backwards from its proof: the class first rebuilds the whole chain from memory (Slides 1–2), then closes the one story Session 9 deliberately left open — how money ends (Slides 3–8) — then spends its centre on a case it has never seen, judged with no help (Slides 9–11), and graduates by owning the lifecycle and the roles outright (Slide 12). The only genuinely new content is money's end, and even that is mostly Session 9's loose threads tied off: the unfixed rejection, the unmatched chain payment, and the unexplained loss from the staircase's last step.

  • Retrieval is the curriculum. The opener corrects only the order of the telling, never the wording — because sequence is what understanding looks like in this trade, and phrasing was never the point.
  • The case is a stranger's house on purpose. Familiarity lets memory impersonate judgment. The unseen case strips the back-story away so only transferable skill remains: permission, proof, honest tests, honest math.
  • The verdict is HOLD, not REJECT — because everything wrong with the file is fixable with evidence, and because the headline failure is uncertainty, not misconduct. Teaching the difference between “stop, this may be someone's home” and “throw it away” is the session's moral centre.
  • The Update Line is graded as hard as the verdict. In the real job the line is what the next desk acts on; a correct verdict buried in forty rambling words changes nothing.

What isn't proven — the open questions, honestly

  • The unseen case and both worked money examples (the staircase recalled from Session 9 and the 500 / 300 / 200 adjustment) are synthetic teaching examples, labelled as such on their slides. They demonstrate the programme's rules; they are not records of real jobs, and no real client, work-order number, address, amount, or crew appears anywhere on this page.
  • The sixty-day payment window is this operation's standing rule for the clients in question, not an industry law; other rulebooks run other clocks, and the slide says so.
  • The six loss reason codes are the programme's one unified list; older drafts carried an UNKNOWN code, which is folded into UNEXPLAINED. The page teaches the unified list only.
  • The property-level adjustment is taught with its guards attached — same property, address-matched, owner-approved before booking. The page does not authorise anyone to book one; it teaches how the decision is made and who makes it.
  • The capstone pass standard (all four failures named, Update Line passing all four checks) is the programme's standard, and the blueprint itself notes the teacher may adjust it. This page presents it as the default, not as an exam regulation — a graded hiring exam attaches later only if the teacher asks for it.
  • Ready For Office belongs to the owner, and submission waits for the owner's word after his cross-check. That is a standing rule of this operation, taught as such — the page never presents it as a client rule.

Running the class from this page

  • Open cold, and stay quiet. Slides 1–2 are a test before they are a welcome. Prompt with one word when the telling stalls; correct only misplaced links.
  • Protect the writing. If time runs short anywhere, cut discussion — never the unseen case, never the written defence, never the Update Line. They are the graduation proof.
  • Reveal in order. Verdict first (Slide 10), then the four failures one drawer at a time, then the model Update Line (Slide 11) counted aloud together.
  • Praise the honest crew. When the class reaches the failed pressure test, model the reviewer's tone: the crew's honesty is praised, the file is still held. Both things, in that order.
  • End plainly. Checklist, roles, sequence, and the house let go. No speech — the ritual is the ending.
  • Nothing here is real client data — the houses are teaching characters, every case is labelled synthetic, and every rule is taught as the programme's rule or the rulebook on the order, never as universal law.

Where it all came from

Every number on the slides names its home in its drawer. In short:

  • The whole session — retrieval journey, money's end, the unseen case with its evidence, expert verdict, next steps, Update Line, pass standard, lifecycle, and role lines: the programme's own Session 10 blueprint (“Money's End + Judgment: The Capstone”) in the class blueprint file.
  • The staircase recalled on Slide 3 (bid 1,000 → allowable 800 → approved 700 → invoiced 700 → paid 550, with the last-step split of 60 / 50 / 40): Session 9 of the same blueprint, a labelled synthetic example in both places.
  • The historical figures recalled on Slide 2 (1972, 2005, 2009 starts; the boom babies; the two 2010 agency piles): proven with sources in the drawers of Classes 1–4 — U.S. Census Bureau housing-starts series, Fannie Mae, and Freddie Mac respectively — and recalled here, not re-proven.
  • The standing rules (sixty-day lag, address-first matching, the unified reason codes, owner-only Ready For Office, submission on the owner's word, office engine vs client portal): the programme's standing rules as recorded in the blueprint's front matter and Session 9–10 text.

This is the demo version of Class 10 from the preservation training programme — shared so the teacher can look it over before the full class is built. Our house is a teaching character, made up for the story; the pictures are illustrations, not a real property. Every case and worked example on this page is a labelled teaching example — no real clients, work orders, addresses, amounts, or company details anywhere on the page.
